titulo: 'The Open Boat' by Stephen Crane, Part One

fuente.licencia: Dominio público (VOA, gobierno de EE. UU.)
fuente.nota: Texto recortado por párrafos; sin cambios en las frases.

parrafos: Our story today is called “The Open Boat.” It was written by Stephen Crane and is based on what really happened to him in eighteen ninety-six.

Crane was traveling from the United States to Cuba as a newspaper reporter. One night, his ship hit a sandbar. It sank in the Atlantic Ocean, off the coast of Florida. Most of the people on board got into lifeboats. Crane was among the last to leave. There were three others with him: the ship’s captain, the cook, and a sailor.

These four men climbed into the only remaining lifeboat. The boat was so small that no one believed it could stay afloat for very long. None of the four men thought he would ever reach the shore. But the men fought the seas bravely, with all their strength. Would they finally reach land? Here is Shep O’Neal with the first part of the story.
The small lifeboat bounced from wave to wave in the rough seas of the Atlantic. The four men in the boat could not see the sky. The waves rose too high.

The waves with their white tops pushed at the open boat with angry violence. Every man thought each wave would be his last. Surely, the boat would sink and he would drown. The men thought that most adults would need a bathtub larger than the boat they were sailing. The waves were huge, and each created a problem in guiding the direction of the boat.
For two days, since the ship sank, the four men had been struggling to reach land. But there was no land to be seen. All the men saw were violent waves which rose and came fiercely down on them.
The men sat in the boat, wondering if there was any hope for them. The ship’s cook sat in the bottom of the boat. He kept looking at the fifteen centimeters which separated him from the ocean.

The boat had only two wooden oars. They were so thin – it seemed as if they would break against the waves. The sailor, named Billie, directed the boat’s movement with one of the oars. The newspaper reporter pulled the second oar. He wondered why he was there in the boat.

The fourth man was the captain of the ship that had sunk. He lay in the front of the small boat. His arm and leg were hurt when the ship sank. The captain’s face was sad. He had lost his ship and many of his sailors. But he looked carefully ahead, and he told Billie when to turn the boat.

Sitting in the boat was like sitting on a wild horse. As each wave came, the boat rose and fell, like a horse starting toward a fence too high to jump. The problem was that after successfully floating over one wave you find that there is another one behind it just as strong and ready to flood your boat.
As each wall of water came in, it hid everything else that the men could see. The waves came in silence; only their white tops made threatening noises.

In the weak light, the faces of the men must have looked gray. Their eyes must have shone in strange ways as they looked out at the sea. The sun rose slowly into the sky. The men knew it was the middle of the day because the color of the sea changed from slate gray to emerald green, with gold lights. And the white foam on the waves looked like falling snow.

As the lifeboat bounced from the top of each wave, the wind tore through the hair of the men. As the boat dropped down again the water fell just past them. The top of each wave was a hill, from which the men could see, for a brief period, a wide area of shining sea.

The cook said the men were lucky because the wind was blowing toward the shore. If it started blowing the other way, they would never reach land. The reporter and the sailor agreed. But the captain laughed in a way that expressed humor and tragedy all in one. He asked: “Do you think we’ve got much of a chance now, boys?”
This made the others stop talking. To express any hope at this time they felt to be childish and stupid. But they also did not want to suggest there was no hope. So they were silent.

Seagulls flew near and far. Sometimes the birds sat down on the sea in groups, near brown seaweed that rolled on the waves. The anger of the sea was no more to them than it was to a group of chickens a thousand miles away on land. Often the seagulls came very close and stared at the men with black bead-like eyes. The men shouted angrily at them, telling them to be gone.

It would be difficult to describe the brotherhood of men that was here established on the sea. Each man felt it warmed him. They were a captain, a sailor, a cook and a reporter. And they were friends. The reporter knew even at the time that this friendship was the best experience of his life.
“I wish we had a sail,” he said, “to give you two boys a chance to rest.” So they used his coat and one of the oars to make a sail and the boat moved much more quickly.

The lighthouse had been slowly growing larger. At last, from the top of each wave the men in the boat could see land. Slowly, the land seemed to rise from the sea. Soon, the men could see two lines, one black and one white.
They knew that the black line was formed by trees, and the white line was the sand. At last, the captain saw a house on the shore. And the lighthouse became even larger.
Slowly and beautifully, the land rose from the sea. The wind came again. Finally, the men heard a new sound – the sound of waves breaking and crashing on the shore.
The men watched the shore grow larger. They became hopeful. In an hour, perhaps, they would be on land. The men struggled to keep the boat from turning over.
They were used to balancing in the boat. Now they rode this wild horse of a boat like circus men. The water poured over them.
titulo_es: «El bote abierto», de Stephen Crane (primera parte)
resumen_es: Adaptación del relato de Stephen Crane, basado en su propio naufragio de 1896: cuatro hombres luchan contra el oleaje en un pequeño bote salvavidas frente a Florida hasta que por fin divisan la costa.
nivel_motivo: Aunque el vocabulario es sencillo, el relato literario usa imágenes, comparaciones y estilo indirecto libre que exigen una comprensión de nivel B2.

ideas_clave.idea: The story draws on Stephen Crane's real experience in 1896, when the ship taking him to Cuba as a journalist sank off Florida.
Crane ended up in the last lifeboat with the captain, the cook and a sailor, none of whom expected to survive.
For two days the tiny boat was battered by enormous waves, and land was nowhere in sight.
Each man had a role: the cook sat in the bottom, the sailor and the reporter handled the two fragile oars, and the injured, grieving captain gave directions.
Riding the waves felt like being on a wild horse, since every wave overcome was followed by another just as dangerous.
The men could only tell the time of day by the changing colours of the sea, and from the crests they briefly glimpsed a wide expanse of water.
When the cook mentioned their luck with the wind, the captain's bitter question about their chances silenced the others, who neither wanted to hope nor to despair.
Indifferent seagulls floated around them, and their calm contrasted with the men's desperate situation.
A deep comradeship grew among the four men, which the reporter considered the best experience of his life, and they improvised a sail with his coat and an oar.
Gradually a lighthouse, trees, a beach and a house came into view, and the men heard the surf breaking on the shore.
Now hopeful of landing within an hour, they fought to keep the boat upright as water poured over them.

resumen_modelo:
The text is an adaptation of a short story by Stephen Crane, inspired by his own shipwreck in 1896. While travelling to Cuba as a newspaper correspondent, Crane saw his ship sink off the coast of Florida, and he ended up in the last lifeboat together with the captain, the cook and a sailor. None of them believed such a tiny craft could survive for long.

For two days the four men struggled against huge, violent waves that hid the sky and threatened to overturn them at any moment. Each had a task: the sailor steered and the reporter rowed with the only two flimsy oars, while the captain, injured and saddened by the loss of his ship and crew, lay in the bow giving directions. The narrator compares the experience to riding a wild horse, since every wave overcome was immediately followed by another equally dangerous one.

Despair and hope alternated. When the captain ironically asked whether they stood much of a chance, the others preferred to remain silent, and even the seagulls seemed indifferent to their plight. Nevertheless, a strong sense of brotherhood developed among them, which the reporter regarded as the finest experience of his life. Thanks to a makeshift sail, the boat gained speed, and eventually a lighthouse, trees, a beach and a house appeared on the horizon. As they heard the surf, the men grew hopeful, although they still had to fight to keep the boat afloat.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Crane was travelling to Cuba as a newspaper reporter when his ship sank.
preguntas.cita: Crane was traveling from the United States to Cuba as a newspaper reporter.
preguntas.explicacion: El párrafo 1 dice expresamente que Crane viajaba a Cuba como reportero de un periódico y que el barco se hundió frente a Florida.

preguntas.pregunta: What caused the ship to sink?
opciones: It was caught in a hurricane.
preguntas.cita: One night, his ship hit a sandbar. It sank in the Atlantic Ocean
preguntas.explicacion: El texto dice que el barco chocó con un banco de arena. No se mencionan huracanes, choques con otro barco ni incendios.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The four men were confident that their lifeboat would reach the shore.
preguntas.cita: None of the four men thought he would ever reach the shore.
preguntas.explicacion: Es al revés: ninguno de los cuatro creía que llegaría a la costa, porque el bote era demasiado pequeño.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 2 una palabra que signifique «a flote, sin hundirse».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'floating on the water, not sinking'.
preguntas.cita: no one believed it could stay afloat for very long
preguntas.explicacion: «Afloat» significa «a flote»; aparece en la expresión «stay afloat», mantenerse a flote.

preguntas.pregunta: How long had the men been trying to reach land at this point of the story?
preguntas.cita: For two days, since the ship sank, the four men had been struggling to reach land.
preguntas.explicacion: El párrafo 5 indica que llevaban dos días luchando por llegar a tierra desde el hundimiento; las demás duraciones no aparecen.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The lifeboat had four strong oars, one for each man.
preguntas.cita: The boat had only two wooden oars. They were so thin – it seemed as if they would break against the waves.
preguntas.explicacion: El bote solo tenía dos remos de madera, y además eran tan finos que parecía que iban a romperse.

preguntas.pregunta: What did the captain do in the boat?
opciones: He told the sailor when to turn the boat.
He rowed with the second oar.
He sat in the bottom of the boat watching the water.
He slept because of his injuries.
respuestas: He told the sailor when to turn the boat.
preguntas.cita: But he looked carefully ahead, and he told Billie when to turn the boat.
preguntas.explicacion: El capitán, herido, iba tumbado delante y le decía a Billie cuándo girar. Quien remaba era el reportero, el que iba en el fondo era el cocinero, y no se dice que durmiera.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 10 una palabra que signifique «amenazadores».
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'menacing, suggesting danger'.
preguntas.cita: only their white tops made threatening noises
preguntas.explicacion: «Threatening» significa «amenazador»; describe el ruido de las crestas blancas de las olas.

preguntas.pregunta: How did the men know that it was the middle of the day?
opciones: The colour of the sea changed.
The captain looked at his watch.
respuestas: The colour of the sea changed.
preguntas.cita: The men knew it was the middle of the day because the color of the sea changed from slate gray to emerald green
preguntas.explicacion: Lo deducían por el cambio de color del mar, de gris pizarra a verde esmeralda. No se habla de relojes, y las gaviotas y el viento aparecen en otros contextos.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: According to the cook, the wind was blowing in a favourable direction.
preguntas.cita: The cook said the men were lucky because the wind was blowing toward the shore.
preguntas.explicacion: El cocinero dice que tienen suerte porque el viento sopla hacia la costa, es decir, en una dirección favorable.

preguntas.pregunta: Why did the men remain silent after the captain's question?
respuestas: They felt that expressing hope would be childish and foolish in their situation, but they did not want to admit that there was no hope either, so they said nothing.
preguntas.cita: To express any hope at this time they felt to be childish and stupid. But they also did not want to suggest there was no hope.
preguntas.explicacion: El párrafo 14 explica el dilema: mostrar esperanza parecía infantil, pero tampoco querían dar a entender que no la había.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o si el texto no lo dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: The men caught a seagull and ate it.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto solo dice que las gaviotas se acercaban y que los hombres les gritaban para que se fueran; no menciona que cazaran ni comieran ninguna.

preguntas.pregunta: What positive experience did the reporter have in the boat, despite the danger?
respuestas: He experienced a deep sense of brotherhood and friendship with the other three men, which he recognised, even at the time, as the best experience of his life.
preguntas.cita: The reporter knew even at the time that this friendship was the best experience of his life.
preguntas.explicacion: El párrafo 16 describe la hermandad que surge entre los cuatro hombres y dice que el reportero la consideró la mejor experiencia de su vida.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 17 una palabra que signifique «vela» (de barco).
preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'a piece of cloth that catches the wind to move a boat'.
preguntas.cita: they used his coat and one of the oars to make a sail
preguntas.explicacion: «Sail» es la vela de una embarcación; la improvisan con el abrigo del reportero y un remo.

preguntas.pregunta: What did the black line and the white line on the horizon represent?
preguntas.cita: They knew that the black line was formed by trees, and the white line was the sand.
preguntas.explicacion: La línea negra eran los árboles y la blanca, la arena. Las otras opciones mezclan elementos que el texto no asocia con esas líneas.

preguntas.pregunta: How does the mood of the men change at the end of this part of the story?
respuestas: They move from despair to hope: after seeing the land and hearing the surf, they think they might reach the shore within an hour, although they still have to struggle to keep the boat from capsizing.
preguntas.cita: They became hopeful. In an hour, perhaps, they would be on land.
preguntas.explicacion: Los párrafos 21 y 22 muestran que, al ver crecer la costa, los hombres recuperan la esperanza, aunque siguen luchando para que el bote no vuelque.

tribunal.pregunta: Who were the four men in the lifeboat, and how did they end up there?
tribunal.pista_es: Comprensión básica: identificar a los personajes y la situación inicial.
ideas: Crane was a reporter travelling to Cuba in 1896
the ship hit a sandbar and sank off Florida
the captain, the cook and the sailor Billie were with him

tribunal.pregunta: How does the author convey the danger and the violence of the sea?
tribunal.pista_es: Analizar los recursos literarios: comparaciones e imágenes.
ideas: the comparison with a wild horse
the boat is smaller than a bathtub
waves described as walls of water
the changing colours of the sea

tribunal.pregunta: What is the role of the seagulls in this part of the story?
tribunal.pista_es: Interpretar un símbolo: la indiferencia de la naturaleza.
ideas: the birds are indifferent to the men's suffering
contrast between nature's calm and human fear
the men react with anger

tribunal.pregunta: Why do you think the reporter considered the brotherhood in the boat the best experience of his life?
tribunal.pista_es: Opinión razonada sobre la solidaridad en situaciones extremas.
ideas: shared danger removes social differences
cooperation is necessary for survival
a captain, a sailor, a cook and a reporter become equals

tribunal.pregunta: To what extent does the fact that the story is based on real events change the way we read it?
tribunal.pista_es: Reflexionar sobre la relación entre periodismo, experiencia personal y literatura.
ideas: Crane was a journalist who turned his experience into fiction
realism and credibility
literature as a way of making sense of trauma

tribunal.pregunta: Shipwrecks and dangerous sea crossings are still in the news today. Can you relate this story to current events in Spain or the European Union?
tribunal.pista_es: Relacionar el texto con la actualidad: migración marítima y salvamento en el Mediterráneo y el Atlántico.
ideas: migrant boats on the Canary Islands route
search and rescue at sea and the role of states and NGOs
EU migration and border policy

tribunal.pregunta: Maritime transport carries most of world trade. What lessons about safety and risk at sea are still relevant for the shipping industry?
tribunal.pista_es: Llevar el tema al terreno económico: transporte marítimo, seguridad y comercio internacional.
ideas: international safety rules for ships
insurance and the cost of maritime risk
importance of shipping routes for trade

glosario.nota: Colocación habitual: stay afloat (mantenerse a flote), también en sentido figurado para empresas.
Se usa para morir ahogado en el agua; no confundir con choke (atragantarse).
Ortografía estadounidense; en británico, slate grey.

glosario.significado: como cuentas (de collar), pequeños y brillantes
